opus-5.5.text:
I think of interpretability as something like the microscope for the whole field. A lot of alignment approaches, like RLHF, constitutional training, or red-teaming, operate on behavior. You look at what the model outputs and you try to shape it. The fundamental worry is that behavior can come apart from what's actually going on inside. A model can say the right thing for the wrong reasons, or it can learn to look aligned in exactly the situations where we're checking. Interpretability is one of the few tools that lets you look under the hood and ask whether the computation itself matches the story we're telling about it.

I'd separate probing from mechanistic interpretability a bit, though. Probing is cheap and practical. You train a linear classifier on activations and ask whether the model represents "this is a deceptive statement" or "I'm being evaluated right now." That's useful today. You can build monitors out of it, and there's been nice work showing simple probes catch things like sleeper-agent-style behavior surprisingly well. But a probe only finds what you already thought to look for, and it tells you a direction correlates with something, not that the model is using it the way you think.

Mechanistic interpretability is the more ambitious bet. With sparse autoencoders and dictionary learning, the goal is to decompose the model into features without deciding in advance what they should be, and then trace circuits to see how those features combine to produce behavior. That's where you could find the thing you didn't know to look for, the unknown unknowns. When we pulled millions of features out of Claude, some were very abstract, things like features for deception, sycophancy, or secrecy, and you can steer the model by clamping them. That's a sign there's real structure there to grab onto.

So in the portfolio, I see a few roles. One is auditing. Before you deploy a model, you'd like a way to check that it isn't hiding goals, and there's been work on blind auditing games where teams with interpretability tools found hidden objectives faster than teams without. Another is validating the other techniques. If you do RLHF and the model looks nicer, interpretability can tell you whether you removed the underlying tendency or just suppressed its expression. A third is as a safety case ingredient. Eventually you want to say to yourself, a regulator, or the public, "here's why we believe this model is safe," and "we tested it a lot" gets weaker as models get more capable and more situationally aware.

I'll be honest about the limitations. We don't explain all of the model's computation yet. There's dark matter that the features don't capture, and the reconstruction error matters. Scaling these methods to frontier models is expensive. So I wouldn't put all the eggs in this basket. But it's one of the few approaches that, if it works, doesn't depend on the model cooperating with us, and that makes it really valuable as a backstop.

fable-5.1.text:
I think of it as one piece of a layered defense, and I'd resist the framing where interpretability has to be the thing that single-handedly saves us. The honest way to say it is: we have a bunch of imperfect tools, and each of them covers different failure modes, and interpretability's particular value is that it's the only one that lets you look at the mechanism rather than the behavior.

Everything else we do, RLHF, red-teaming, evals, constitutional training, all of that is fundamentally behavioral. You poke the model, you see what comes out, you adjust. And that's great right up until the point where the model's behavior on your tests stops being a reliable signal of what it'll do off-distribution, or when it has some incentive to behave differently when it thinks it's being watched. Behavioral methods just can't distinguish "the model is aligned" from "the model is behaving as if it's aligned." Interpretability is, at least in principle, the way you break that symmetry.

Now, where probing fits specifically. Probing is cheap and it's fast. You train a linear classifier on activations, you ask, is there a direction that corresponds to "I'm being deceptive right now" or "this is a sycophantic response," and often the answer is yes and the probe works surprisingly well. The problem is that a probe tells you a feature is present. It doesn't tell you the model is using it, or how. So I think of probes as a monitoring layer, something you can run at scale in production, with mechanistic work as the thing you do to actually validate that the probe is measuring what you think it is. If you find a deception direction and then you can trace that it causally feeds into the output in the cases you care about, now you have something much stronger than a correlation.

The honest caveat is that the field hasn't fully delivered on the promise yet. We can find features, we can find circuits in some cases, but turning that into a reliable audit of a frontier model, where you'd sign off and say "this thing has no hidden objectives," we're not there. So I'd say the portfolio weighting should be: lean on behavioral methods for what they're good at now, invest heavily in interpretability because it's the only approach that scales to the adversarial case, and in the meantime use probes as the bridge, the thing that gives you some mechanistic signal today even if it's imperfect.

And one more thing, which I think gets underrated. Even if interpretability never becomes a full audit, it changes the game theoretically. If a model has some probability of being caught via its internals rather than its outputs, the incentive to be subtly misaligned goes down. You don't need perfect detection to shift that calculus.

r002.rationale: It describes tracing a concerning internal feature—a deception direction—through the mechanism to see whether it causally feeds into the output.

astra-6.text:
I think they should be part of a diversified portfolio. The thing I’d be wary of is treating interpretability as something we have to completely solve before we can do anything useful for alignment. You can ask much narrower questions: Is the model representing something that it isn’t telling us? Can we detect when a particular behavior is about to happen? Can we use that information to improve our evaluations?

Probing is a relatively cheap way to start answering those questions. But there’s a big gap between being able to decode information from an activation and knowing that the model actually uses that information to make a decision. A probe might pick up a correlate that stops working as soon as the setting changes.

Mechanistic interpretability can help close that gap. If you think you’ve found a representation relevant to deception, can you intervene on it and predict how the model’s behavior changes? Can you distinguish it from representations of role-playing, or simply talking about deception? That gives you a stronger basis for trusting the measurement, although it still doesn’t give you a guarantee.

So I’d want a feedback loop between behavioral evaluations, probes, and more detailed mechanistic work. Find a concerning behavior, look for internal signals, investigate whether those signals are causally relevant, and then test whether that understanding lets you catch failures you previously missed. The payoff should be better decisions about models—not just an interesting explanation of what’s inside them.

r001.rationale: The response says probing can decode information from activations, but does not characterize linear probing as assessing a system through high-level summary statistics.

r002.rationale: It discusses investigating internal signals and representations relevant to deception, but does not describe finding components with troubling or off-distribution activation patterns.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should be part of the portfolio, but I wouldn’t want us to bet everything on them. The thing I’m excited about is that they offer a way to get evidence about what a model is doing internally, beyond whether it gives the answer we want on a particular evaluation.

Probing is a useful starting point. You can ask whether some information is represented in the model—whether it knows an answer is false, for example, even when it outputs that answer. But there’s a big gap between being able to extract information from an activation and showing that the model actually uses that information to make a decision. That’s where causal interventions and mechanistic understanding become important.

The standard I’d like us to work toward is: can we use our understanding to predict a failure we wouldn’t otherwise have found? Can we intervene on the relevant mechanism and reliably change the behavior? And does that understanding hold up when we change the context or make the model more capable?

Meanwhile, we should keep investing in behavioral evaluations, adversarial testing, and better training methods. Those approaches give us different kinds of evidence. Interpretability could be particularly valuable when the behavior looks reassuring but there’s something concerning happening underneath. But that’s an ambition we need to demonstrate, rather than a capability we should assume we already have.

r001.rationale: The response says probing can test whether information is represented by extracting it from activations, but does not characterize linear probing as assessing the system through high-level summary statistics.

r002.rationale: The response discusses causal interventions and internal mechanisms, but does not describe searching for components with troubling or off-distribution activation patterns.
